name: Standard Scramble
gear: ice axe (glacier remnant and permanent snow near the col make this needed in every season, not just early season)
30m rope (optional, for the crux band or a rappel if conditions warrant)
hazards: loose, blocky rock on the cliff bands below the Two-Main col
exposed fourth-class climbing on the crux band beside the wet summit chimney
route-finding among towers and cliff bands with no cairns or markers
a snow/rock moat and occasional crevasses on the small Lemah Glacier remnant, more difficult to cross late season
faint, brushy, unmaintained climbers' trail along Lemah Creek with deadfall and a slide-alder thicket near camp
a long summit day; many parties finish the descent to camp after dark
overview: Lemah Two (7,280 ft) is the second-highest of five distinct summits along the serrated, mile-long Lemah crest — Lemah One (6,960'), Lemah Two (7,280'), the Main/Lemah Three summit (7,512', the massif's true high point), Lemah Four (7,200'), and Lemah Five (7,040') — rising above Spectacle Lake and Pete Lake in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Part of the Snoqualmie Crest section of the North Cascades roughly 7.7 miles east of Snoqualmie Pass, the massif carries a small remnant glacier (Lemah Glacier) on its east face. Lemah Two is typically climbed as a natural add-on from the col shared with the main summit, or as a standalone objective for parties working through the multi-peaked massif.
beta: From the Lemah Creek meadow (~3,600 ft), traverse toward the base of the peaks and climb a series of Class 2-3 cliff bands toward the col between Lemah Two and the Main Peak (Lemah Three). A snow slope and chute lead up to the col; the chute itself -- a mix of steep snow/ice and Class 3-4 rock, often with water running down it -- is the technical crux. Crampons and an ice axe are commonly used even in summer. From the col, a short 3rd/4th-class rock section leads to Lemah Two's summit.
turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time based on your party's pace, snow conditions, and forecast -- the crux chute and cliff bands become more hazardous to downclimb once afternoon sun softens snow or exposes wet rock, and this is a long day with a long walk out.
rappels: Some parties place a single rappel down the crux chute on one rope length rather than downclimbing wet rock; otherwise the route is reversed by downclimbing.
permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
comms: This is a deep, remote section of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness; expect no reliable cell coverage in the Lemah Creek valley or on the peak. A satellite communicator or PLB is recommended for emergencies.
descent: Reverse the ascent: downclimb from the summit back to the col, then down the chute and its Class 3-4 band, re-cross the moat onto the glacier remnant, and descend the snow/glacier back to about 5,000 ft and on to camp. Summit day is long, and parties frequently finish the descent to camp after dark — carry headlamps and know the crux downclimb before committing.
obj_haz: Rockfall/loose rock ("choss") in the summit gully and buttress
Minor crevasses on the remnant Lemah Glacier
Steep snow/ice up to ~45° in the summit chute
Moat crossing at the glacier margin
Dense brush/bushwhacking on the lower approach

detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is required for the standard line -- most parties carry an ice axe and crampons for the snow slope/chute below the col, plus a helmet for the loose cliff-band terrain. A light rack (a few slings/a short rope) is sometimes carried in case a party wants to rappel the crux chute rather than downclimb it.
pro_tips: many parties tag Lemah Two as a side trip while climbing the main summit, since both share the same approach to the Two/Main col
the meadow camp at ~3,600 ft has better tent sites past the slide-alder band in the timber to the north, away from the crowded Pete Lake shoreline
carry a rope and light rack for the crux band even though most of the route is scrambling, especially if snow or verglas coats the rock
watch_out: the unmarked climbers' trail leaving the PCT on the north side of Lemah Creek is easy to miss and easy to lose again once on it
the wet rock chimney at the col often has water (or verglas in cool weather) running down it even in summer
downclimbing the Class 3-4 band above the glacier remnant in the dark on the return
pro_needs: Minimal fixed protection is used; this is an unroped scramble/snow climb for most parties rather than a pitched rock route. Ice axe and crampons substitute for rock protection on the summit snow/ice chute.
approach: From I-90 exit 80 (Roslyn/Salmon la Sac), drive north on SR-903 for 16.8 miles through Roslyn and past Cle Elum Lake, then west on Forest Road 46 for 4.7 miles and right on FR-4616 for 1 mile to the Cooper Lake/Pete Lake trailhead. Follow the Pete Lake Trail #1323 along the Cooper River about 4 miles to Pete Lake, continue past the lake about 1.2 miles to the PCT, then turn right (north) on the PCT for about a mile to the Lemah Creek crossing, where a faint, unmaintained climbers' trail leaves on the north side of Lemah Creek (marked by occasional flagging; expect deadfall/brush for the first ~400 vertical feet). This path passes a series of waterfalls and swimming holes before reaching a meadow at roughly 3,600 ft where the creek breaks into shallow ponds — a common camp, though a thick band of slide alder guards the far end and is best bypassed through the timber to the north. From camp, follow the drainage up to about 5,000 ft where the Lemah Glacier remnant begins, climb to roughly 6,200 ft, exit south (climber's left) up a short cliff onto glacial remnants on the peak's southeast side, then traverse northwest toward the base of the Main Peak/Lemah Two col.
descent_text: From the traverse below Main Peak, climb a series of Class 2-3 cliff bands toward the col between Lemah Two and Lemah Main. A moat typically separates the glacier remnant from the rock here, worse late season — exit the snow below and right of an obvious wet rock chimney, then climb mostly Class 3 with a short Class 4 step to the chimney's right to reach the col. From the col, turn south and finish on the short 3rd/4th-class rock section to Lemah Two's summit.
bail: Retreat is possible at essentially any point on the cliff bands or col below the summit by reversing the ascent line back down to the Lemah Creek meadow; there are no fixed bail anchors, so retreat means downclimbing (or rappelling) the same terrain just climbed.

pitch_detail.notes: ~4 miles, mostly flat forest trail along the Cooper River.
Climber's path on the north side of the creek past waterfalls and swimming holes to the ~3,600 ft meadow.

itinerary.cal: The SE face chute crux is typically climbed as a snow feature and is most straightforward early-mid summer (roughly late June-August) before it melts out to bare rock/ice; check current trip reports for snow coverage before committing to the standard line.

days.note: From the Cooper Lake trailhead, follow the mellow Cooper River / Pete Lake Trail (~4 mi) to Pete Lake, continue to the PCT junction, then head north on the PCT about a mile to the Lemah Creek crossing. Leave the trail before the footbridge and work up along Lemah Creek roughly a mile cross-country to a bench/meadow camp (commonly cited around 4,000-4,500 ft, sometimes lower near 3,600 ft at the Lemah Meadows/PCT junction).

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day standard trip is typical: ~16 miles round trip with roughly 5,000 ft of total gain/loss, one (sometimes two) nights camped near Lemah Creek, and a long glacier/snow-chute summit day; strong parties compress the summit push and hike-out into one big day for a 2-day version instead.

access.notes: Climbable roughly June–October; heavy winter snowfall and frequent avalanche control closures on I-90 affect access the rest of the year.

climate.typical: Approach and route are generally snow-free late July through September; permanent snow/ice on the small Lemah Glacier remnant near the Two-Main col means an ice axe and crampons are recommended in every season, not just early season.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass zone (nearest official NWAC avalanche forecast zone; Lemah sits ~7.7 mi east of Snoqualmie Pass)

emergency.notes: No cell coverage in the Lemah Creek valley; this is a remote, rarely-patrolled wilderness route. Self-rescue capability and a satellite communicator are strongly recommended.
emergency.rangerStation: Cle Elum Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest
emergency.nearestHospital: Kittitas Valley Healthcare, 603 S Chestnut St, Ellensburg, WA — Cle Elum only has urgent-care/family-medicine clinics, no ER, so Ellensburg is the nearest full hospital

crowds.peakTraffic: Rare even in-season; mostly visited as part of a Lemah crest traverse or a dedicated multi-day scramble trip, occasional July-August weekends
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very low - likely only a handful to low dozens of parties per season

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very high - long approach with significant off-trail travel, elevation gain, and at least one stream crossing (Lemah Creek); typically done as an overnight or multi-day trip rather than a day push
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/multi-day pack (camp gear + several days food) is typical given the remote approach into the Lemah basin

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long, multi-day approach - roughly 8 miles one-way via the Pete Lake Trail to the Spectacle Lake/Lemah Meadows area, plus additional off-trail travel to gain the Lemah crest and traverse to Lemah Two; most parties camp in the Lemah basin rather than attempting it as a single day push
requiredSkills: route-finding on loose rock among towers
judgment for short exposed steps that may warrant a handline
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine scrambler comfortable with exposed Class 4 terrain, loose rock, and route-finding among towers; prior Cascades scrambling experience strongly recommended before attempting the Lemah crest

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through September, with August the most reliable month; consistent dry-rock conditions typically don't arrive until late July

July.reason: Route only comes into season late in the month; early July can still have lingering snow on the approach and summit ledges

August.reason: In season; driest rock and most stable maritime-summer weather for the exposed fourth-class terrain

September.reason: Still within the season window with a short clear weather stretch, but shortening days and the first fall weather systems reduce the margin versus August

weather.typical: Maritime Cascades climate - clearest and driest in mid-to-late summer, with full winter conditions and snow cover outside the scramble season
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a possibility during the July-August window typical of Cascade summer weather

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Exposed fourth-class climbing on ledges and short steps with loose rock; route-finding among towers is a real risk of getting cliffed out, and a fall on the exposed sections would be serious

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer route (nearest NWAC forecast zone is Snoqualmie Pass, used only as a general regional proxy since this route is not climbed in avalanche season)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: The route crosses the small Lemah Glacier remnant en route to the Two-Main col; a snow/rock moat and occasional crevasses form at the glacier-to-rock transition, harder to negotiate late season - carry glacier travel gear and rope up if crevasses are open.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and the PCT to the Lemah Creek climbers' path, then the col below the Main Peak
approach_variants.notes:
From I-90 exit 80 at Roslyn / Salmon la Sac, drive SR-903 north 16.8 miles through Roslyn and past Cle Elum Lake, then west on FR-46 for 4.7 miles and right on FR-4616 for a mile to the Cooper Lake / Pete Lake trailhead.

Follow Pete Lake Trail #1323 along the Cooper River about 4 miles to Pete Lake, continue past it about 1.2 miles to the PCT, then turn right (north) on the PCT for about a mile to the Lemah Creek crossing.

A faint, unmaintained climbers' trail leaves on the NORTH side of Lemah Creek, marked by occasional flagging, with deadfall and brush for the first 400 vertical feet. It passes waterfalls and swimming holes and reaches a meadow at about 3,600 ft where the creek breaks into shallow ponds — the common camp. A thick band of slide alder guards the far end of that meadow and is best bypassed through the timber to the north.

About 12.9 km and 4,480 ft.
hazards: A faint, unmaintained climbers' trail with deadfall and brush for the first 400 vertical feet
A thick band of slide alder at the far end of the meadow camp
Steep snow or ice and class 3-4 rock in the crux chute, often with water running down it
A moat where the glacier remnant meets the rock
A long summit day with descents routinely finishing after dark — carry headlamps
Remote terrain with a multi-day walk out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL YOU ARE AIMING FOR IS A COL, AND IT IS THE COL BETWEEN LEMAH TWO AND THE MAIN PEAK. From the 3,600 ft meadow camp, follow the drainage to about 5,000 ft where the Lemah Glacier remnant begins, climb to roughly 6,200 ft, then exit SOUTH — climbers' left — up a short cliff onto glacial remnants on the peak's southeast side, and traverse northwest to the base of that col. The technical ground is the climb up to the col; below that you are walking, scrambling class 2-3 cliff bands, and crossing snow.

THE CONFIRMING FEATURE BELOW THE COL IS A CHUTE, AND ITS CHARACTER IS DISTINCTIVE: a snow slope and then a chute of mixed steep snow or ice and class 3-4 rock, OFTEN WITH WATER RUNNING DOWN IT. Running water in the chute is the signature of this line and is why parties carry crampons and an axe even in summer. That chute is the technical crux of the route.

THE ALTITUDE SEQUENCE IS THE FOG TEST: 3,600 ft camp, 5,000 ft glacier remnant, 6,200 ft, then exit left up a short cliff. Four altimeter checks and one turn, none of which needs the summit to be visible.

AND THE NEGATIVE: if you are climbing toward a summit without having stood in a col between two distinct peaks, you are on the wrong feature. Lemah Two is the second of the Lemah summits and the Main Peak — Lemah Three — is the one across the col from you.

PLAN THE DOWNCLIMB BEFORE YOU COMMIT TO THE CHUTE. Summit day here is long and parties frequently finish the descent to camp after dark.

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
bivy.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each
